title: Home
text: Fast, frame-accurate scene cut detection for video. Detect fast cuts and fades. pip install scenedetect AdaptiveDetector ContentDetector HashDetector HistogramDetector ThresholdDetector split-video ffmpeg mkvmerge Docker.

title: Home
text: People use PySceneDetect for many video workflows: Splitting home videos or raw footage into separate scene clips. Finding and removing commercials from recorded TV broadcasts. Reviewing and splitting security camera recordings. Finding clean loops in videos for GIFs and cinemagraphs. Analyzing film and video datasets, such as measuring average shot length. Download PySceneDetect to try it on your own videos, or review the Features page for a full list of detectors and export formats. The default timecode format ( HH:MM:SS.nnn ) works directly with tools such as ffmpeg and mkvmerge .

title: Features
text: PySceneDetect finds cuts between scenes by comparing frame content, not only fades to black. A threshold detector is also included for detecting fades.

title: Features
text: Export detected scene cuts in formats that work directly with video editors and command-line tools. The default comma-separated HH:MM:SS.nnn format can be pasted directly into ffmpeg or mkvmerge .

title: Features
text: Export frame-by-frame metrics to a CSV stats file so you can plot trends in a spreadsheet and pick the best threshold for your video.

title: Features
text: PySceneDetect is written in Python with an extensible API. You can embed it in your own applications or write custom detectors for specialized video workflows.

title: Features
text: Export timecodes in comma-separated HH:MM:SS.nnn format for external tools and spreadsheets. Save frame-by-frame video metrics to a CSV stats file with -s FILE / --stats FILE (for example, --stats metrics.csv ). Hide terminal output with -q / --quiet when automating scripts. Save still frames from each scene with the save-images command. Split the input video into separate scene clips with split-video using ffmpeg or mkvmerge .

title: Features
text: CSV ( list-scenes ): save a scene list table and comma-separated cut times ( HH:MM:SS.nnn ). EDL ( save-edl ): save a CMX 3600 edit decision list for most video editors. title: Features
text: PySceneDetect includes five detectors. You can run them alone or combine more than one for the same video: Adaptive detector ( detect-adaptive , default): compares each frame's HSV content score against a rolling average of nearby frames to find fast cuts while reducing false cuts during camera motion. Content detector ( detect-content ): compares differences in the HSV color space (and optional edges) between adjacent frames to find fast cuts. Perceptual hash detector ( detect-hash ): computes a perceptual hash for each frame and compares adjacent hashes to find fast cuts. Histogram detector

title: Features

title: Download
text: PySceneDetect is free, open-source software released under the BSD 3-Clause License (see License & Copyright ). If you have trouble running PySceneDetect, verify that you have the packages listed under Dependencies .

title: Download
text: Windows 64-bit · v0.7.3 November 8, 2026 Installer .msi Recommended Portable .zip The .msi installer is recommended for most Windows users. Both Windows builds bundle ffmpeg . To use split-video -m , install MKVToolNix. After installing, see the Command-Line Interface guide to get started.

title: Download
section: Install with pip, uv, or pipx
text: Installing from PyPI requires Python 3.10 or newer. Standard install with pip (CLI and Python API): pip install --upgrade scenedetect Headless install (for servers and containers without GUI libraries): pip install --upgrade scenedetect-headless Install with uv or pipx : # uv (isolated CLI tool) uv tool install scenedetect # uv (add to a Python project) uv add scenedetect # pipx (isolated CLI tool) pipx install scenedetect PySceneDetect is published on PyPI as two packages, both including the CLI and the scenedetect Python module: scenedetect : depends on opencv-python . scenedetect-headless :

title: Download
text: Official container images are published on GitHub Container Registry at ghcr.io/breakthrough/pyscenedetect . Each image includes the CLI, all optional video backends (PyAV and MoviePy), ffmpeg , and mkvmerge : docker pull ghcr.io/breakthrough/pyscenedetect docker run --rm ghcr.io/breakthrough/pyscenedetect version To process videos, mount the folder that holds them into the container. The container runs as a non-root user, so output files keep normal permissions: docker run --rm -v " $( pwd ) :/files" ghcr.io/breakthrough/pyscenedetect \ -i /files/video.mp4 detect-adaptive split-video -o /file

title: Download
text: After installing, open a terminal and run scenedetect version or scenedetect --help . If you see an import error, verify that import numpy and import cv2 work in Python and review Dependencies . If you find a bug or want to suggest a feature, open an issue on the issue tracker or see Contributing & Support .

title: Download
text: The scenedetect and scenedetect-headless packages install these dependencies automatically: OpenCV : pip install opencv-python (or opencv-python-headless with scenedetect-headless ) NumPy : pip install numpy Click : pip install click (used by the CLI) tqdm : pip install tqdm (displays progress bars) platformdirs : pip install platformdirs (used by the CLI) Optional video backend packages: PyAV : pip install av (or pip install "scenedetect[pyav]" ) MoviePy : pip install moviepy (or pip install "scenedetect[moviepy]" )

title: Download
text: To split videos into clips, install at least one of these tools ( ffmpeg is bundled in the Windows builds; the Docker image has both): FFmpeg : splits videos with re-encoding ( split-video ) or stream copy ( split-video -c / --copy ). MKVToolNix ( mkvmerge ): splits videos in stream-copy mode ( split-video -m / --mkvmerge ). See Video Splitting Requirements for installation and PATH setup steps.

title: Download
text: If you installed OpenCV with pip , uninstall it before installing a different OpenCV build or compiling from source. See the Installing OpenCV guide for steps on Windows and Linux. To verify your setup, open a Python prompt and run import numpy and import cv2 .

title: Command-Line Interface
text: See the Reference Manual for a complete list of scenedetect commands and options.

title: Command-Line Interface
text: Split a video at each fast cut using ffmpeg : scenedetect -i video.mp4 split-video Save still frames from each scene: scenedetect -i video.mp4 save-images Skip the first 10 seconds of the video: scenedetect -i video.mp4 time -s 10s

title: Command-Line Interface
text: This walkthrough uses a short clip from the James Bond film GoldenEye (Copyright © 1995 MGM): Watch the clip on YouTube Download goldeneye.mp4 (right-click and save it in your working directory as goldeneye.mp4 ) To split this clip on each fast cut, use the adaptive detector ( detect-adaptive ) or the content detector ( detect-content ). To detect fades to and from black instead, use detect-threshold . When you do not specify a detector, PySceneDetect uses detect-adaptive by default. Start by saving a CSV scene list and preview images for each scene: scenedetect --input goldeneye.mp4 detect-ad

title: Command-Line Interface
text: Use the split-video command to split the input video with ffmpeg or mkvmerge : scenedetect -i goldeneye.mp4 split-video By default, split-video re-encodes each clip with ffmpeg for frame-accurate cuts. You can adjust encoding quality with -hq / --high-quality (near-lossless), -p / --preset , and -crf / --rate-factor . For faster splitting without re-encoding, pass -c / --copy (uses ffmpeg stream copy) or -m / --mkvmerge (uses mkvmerge ). Stream copy splits only on keyframes, so clip boundaries may not be frame-accurate. Run scenedetect split-video --help for all options.

title: Command-Line Interface
text: PySceneDetect includes five detectors: detect-adaptive (default): finds fast cuts by comparing each frame's content score against a rolling average of nearby frames. detect-content : finds fast cuts by comparing differences in HSV color and optional edges between adjacent frames. detect-hash : finds fast cuts by comparing perceptual hashes of adjacent frames. detect-hist : finds fast cuts by comparing Y-channel (brightness) histograms of adjacent frames. detect-threshold : finds fades to and from black by comparing average frame brightness against a threshold. Most detector options can also be

title: Command-Line Interface
text: detect-adaptive compares each frame's content_val score against the average of nearby frames and records the ratio in the stats file under adaptive_ratio (w=2) (the w= suffix matches --frame-window ). This reduces false cuts during fast camera movement. Adjust the window size with --frame-window and the minimum content score with --min-content-val .

title: Command-Line Interface
text: detect-content measures the difference between each pair of adjacent frames and records a cut when the difference exceeds the threshold (default: 27.0 ). To find the best threshold, generate a stats file with -s , open it in a spreadsheet editor, and check the content_val column ( example ). This value stays low within a scene and spikes when the scene changes. Choose a threshold above normal motion scores and below the spikes at real cuts.

title: Command-Line Interface
text: detect-threshold measures the average RGB brightness of each frame (from 0.0 to 255.0 ) and records a fade event when brightness crosses the threshold. The default threshold is 12.0 : scenedetect -i video.mp4 -s video.stats.csv detect-threshold scenedetect -i video.mp4 -s video.stats.csv detect-threshold -t 20 Thresholds below 8.0 can cause missed detections on videos with low bitrates or limited brightness range. To tune the threshold, generate a stats file with -s and inspect the average_rgb column in a spreadsheet editor. Choose a threshold below the brightness of normal scenes and above th

title: Command-Line Interface
text: You can configure detector options on the command line or in a config file . If the default threshold does not give the results you want, generate a stats file first: scenedetect --input goldeneye.mp4 --stats goldeneye.stats.csv detect-adaptive Then plot the content_val or adaptive_ratio (w=2) column from goldeneye.stats.csv : Peaks in the graph match the scene cuts in the video. For fast-cut detectors, raise the threshold to reduce false cuts or lower it to catch missed cuts. For detect-threshold , do the opposite: raise -t to catch more fades or lower it to reduce false detections.

title: Command-Line Interface
section: Saving Image Previews of Detected Scenes
text: Use save-images to save still frames from each detected scene in your working directory (or the folder set with -o / --output ). By default, save-images saves three JPEG images per scene (start, middle, and end), numbered 01 , 02 , and 03 (for example, goldeneye-Scene-001-01.jpg ). Use -n / --num-images to choose a different fixed count per scene, or -i / --interval to save one image per time interval so longer scenes produce more images. Run scenedetect save-images --help for format, size, and quality options.

title: Command-Line Interface
text: These global options go before any command (such as detect-adaptive or list-scenes ). They speed up processing at the cost of some accuracy: Downscaling ( -d / --downscale ) : shrinks each frame by an integer factor ( 2 , 3 , 4 , and so on) before analysis. By default, PySceneDetect picks a downscale factor automatically based on video resolution. Pass -d 1 to disable downscaling, or a higher integer to process frames faster. Frame skipping ( -fs / --frame-skip ) : skips N frames after every processed frame. For example, --frame-skip 1 processes every second frame and roughly doubles speed. Fr

title: Command-Line Interface
section: Seeking, Duration, and Start / End Times
text: Use the time command to analyze only part of a video. It accepts three options: -s / --start : where to begin detection. -e / --end : where to stop detection. -d / --duration : how much video to process after the start time. Set either --end or --duration , not both. You can write times in seconds ( 100.0 or 100s ), frames ( 100 ), or HH:MM:SS[.nnn] timecode ( 00:05:00.000 ). For a 30 FPS video, all four commands below analyze the same 90-second segment (2700 frames) between 00:05:00 and 00:06:30 : scenedetect -i video.mp4 time --start 00 :05:00 --end 00 :06:30 scenedetect -i video.mp4 time --

title: Command-Line Interface
text: Pass a config file path with -c / --config . If you do not pass -c , PySceneDetect checks for scenedetect.cfg in your platform's default user config folder: Windows: C:/Users/%USERNAME%/AppData/Local/PySceneDetect/scenedetect.cfg Linux: ~/.config/PySceneDetect/scenedetect.cfg $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/PySceneDetect/scenedetect.cfg macOS: ~/Library/Application Support/PySceneDetect/scenedetect.cfg Run scenedetect --help to see the exact path on your system under the -c / --config help text. You can download the scenedetect.cfg template from GitHub , or copy it from the PySceneDetect installation folder

title: Command-Line Interface
text: [global] default-detector = detect-content min-scene-len = 0.8s [detect-content] threshold = 32 weights = 1.0 0.5 1.0 0.2 [split-video] preset = slow rate-factor = 17 # Quotes are not needed even if the filename contains spaces filename = $VIDEO_NAME-Clip-$SCENE_NUMBER [save-images] format = jpeg quality = 80 num-images = 3 See the Configuration File Reference or the scenedetect.cfg template on GitHub for every available key.

title: Command-Line Interface
text: PySceneDetect uses ffmpeg or mkvmerge to split videos: split-video (default): uses ffmpeg and re-encodes for frame-accurate splits. split-video -c / --copy : uses ffmpeg in stream-copy mode. split-video -m / --mkvmerge : uses mkvmerge in stream-copy mode.

title: Command-Line Interface
text: Download ffmpeg from FFmpeg . On Linux, install it with your package manager (for example, sudo apt-get install ffmpeg ). On Windows, the PySceneDetect builds bundle ffmpeg ; otherwise follow the steps below.

title: Command-Line Interface
text: Download mkvmerge as part of MKVToolNix . Use the installer on Windows or your system package manager on Linux so PySceneDetect can find mkvmerge automatically.

title: Command-Line Interface
text: If PySceneDetect cannot find ffmpeg or mkvmerge , use one of these approaches: Add the folder containing ffmpeg or mkvmerge to your system PATH environment variable so it works from any terminal (recommended). Copy ffmpeg or mkvmerge into the same folder where scenedetect is installed (on Windows with pip , typically C:\PythonXY\Scripts ) if you prefer not to edit PATH . Copy the executable into a folder already on PATH if neither of the above is possible.

title: Python API
text: The complete Python API reference is in the Reference Manual . See Documentation Versions for older releases.

title: Python API
text: This page describes how each built-in detector works, along with its key CLI options and default values.

title: Python API
text: The adaptive detector ( AdaptiveDetector / detect-adaptive , default in the CLI) scores adjacent frames the same way as ContentDetector , then compares each frame's score against a rolling average of nearby frames. This reduces false cuts during fast camera movement. Default settings: --threshold 3.0 , --frame-window 2 , --min-content-val 15.0 . See detect-adaptive and AdaptiveDetector for details.

title: Python API
text: The content detector ( ContentDetector / detect-content ) finds fast cuts between scenes. It converts each frame from RGB to HSV , computes the average difference across hue, saturation, and value (brightness) between adjacent frames, and records a cut when that score exceeds --threshold (default: 27.0 ). You can also enable edge detection by passing four weights ( delta_hue , delta_sat , delta_lum , delta_edges ). Edge differences are usually larger than color differences, so raise the threshold when enabling edges (for example, -w 1.0 0.5 1.0 0.2 -t 32 ). The default weights are --weights 1.

title: Python API
text: The perceptual hash detector ( HashDetector / detect-hash ) computes a perceptual hash ( phash , based on imagehash ) for each frame and compares adjacent hashes using normalized Hamming distance. When the distance exceeds --threshold (default: 0.35 , with --size 8 and --lowpass 2 ), it records a cut. Because phash converts frames to grayscale first, HashDetector ignores color changes when brightness stays constant. It is fast even without downscaling. See Looks Like It for a visual explanation of perceptual hashing. See detect-hash and HashDetector for details.

title: Python API
text: The histogram detector ( HistogramDetector / detect-hist ) finds fast cuts using brightness histograms. It converts each frame to the YUV color space, extracts the Y (luminance) channel, and builds a normalized histogram with --bins bins (default: 128 ). Adjacent frame histograms are compared using correlation ( cv2.HISTCMP_CORREL ). When the difference exceeds --threshold (default: 0.20 ), the detector records a cut. Focusing on luminance makes this detector less sensitive to pure color shifts. See detect-hist and HistogramDetector for details.

title: Python API
text: The threshold detector ( ThresholdDetector / detect-threshold ) finds fades to and from black, similar to the ffmpeg blackframe filter. It averages the R, G, and B values of every pixel in each frame to get a brightness score from 0.0 to 255.0 , and records fade events when that score crosses --threshold (default: 12.0 ). See detect-threshold and ThresholdDetector for details.

title: Python API
text: Custom detectors must inherit from SceneDetector . Because the SceneDetector interface may change before v1.0, pin your dependency to a minor version (for example, scenedetect~=0.7.0 ). To create a detector, implement process_frame and, if needed, post_process : import numpy as np from scenedetect import FrameTimecode , SceneDetector class CustomDetector ( SceneDetector ): """Example custom scene detector.""" def process_frame ( self , timecode : FrameTimecode , frame_img : np . ndarray , ) -> list [ FrameTimecode ]: # Return a list of cut timecodes found on this frame or earlier. return [] de

title: Benchmarks
text: PySceneDetect's detectors are tested for accuracy against three public shot-boundary detection datasets. Scoring follows the TRECVID-SBD convention (greedy 1-to-1 nearest-neighbor matching with a configurable frame tolerance for hard cuts, and point-in-interval matching for fades), so results can be compared directly with published research. The benchmark code, dataset loaders, and result summaries ( README.md , SWEEP_REPORT.md ) are in benchmark/ on GitHub. The three datasets cover different types of video: BBC Planet Earth : 11 long-form broadcast episodes (hard cuts only). AutoShot : short

title: Frequently Asked Questions
section: How do I fix ImportError: No module named cv2 ?
text: Since PySceneDetect 0.7, OpenCV is installed automatically. Install the standard package: pip install scenedetect For servers or containers without GUI libraries, install the headless package instead: pip install scenedetect-headless Both packages provide the same scenedetect Python module. Install only one of them. If your project needs a different OpenCV package (such as opencv-contrib-python ), install the exact same version that scenedetect installed so both packages share identical cv2 files: pip install scenedetect pip install "opencv-contrib-python== $( pip show opencv-python | grep ^Ve

title: Frequently Asked Questions
section: How do I enable video splitting?
text: PySceneDetect uses FFmpeg or mkvmerge from MKVToolNix to split videos. Make sure the executable is on your system PATH or in the same folder as scenedetect . The Windows builds include ffmpeg . The Docker image includes both tools. See Video Splitting Requirements for setup steps.

title: Frequently Asked Questions
section: How do I tune the detection threshold?
text: Generate a per-frame stats file with -s / --stats : scenedetect -i video.mp4 -s video.stats.csv detect-adaptive Open video.stats.csv in a spreadsheet tool and inspect the metric column for your detector ( adaptive_ratio (w=2) for detect-adaptive , where the w= suffix matches --frame-window ; content_val for detect-content ; or average_rgb for detect-threshold ). For fast-cut detectors ( detect-adaptive , detect-content , detect-hash , detect-hist ), lower the threshold ( -t ) if PySceneDetect misses real cuts, or raise -t to reduce false cuts. For detect-threshold , do the opposite: raise -t t

title: Frequently Asked Questions
section: Does PySceneDetect support variable frame rate (VFR) videos?
text: Yes. Both the default OpenCV backend and the PyAV backend support VFR videos using presentation timestamps (PTS) instead of assuming a constant frame rate. For difficult VFR files, use the PyAV backend ( pip install av , then pass -b pyav ), which reads native PTS timestamps directly from the video container. The MoviePy backend does not support VFR video. See Video Backends for details.

title: Frequently Asked Questions
section: Should I use stream copy or re-encoding when splitting video?
text: Default re-encoding ( split-video ) : uses ffmpeg to re-encode each clip. Cuts are frame-accurate, and you can adjust quality with -hq / --high-quality , -crf , or -p / --preset . Stream copy ( split-video --copy or split-video --mkvmerge ) : copies the compressed video and audio streams without re-encoding. This is much faster and preserves original quality, but splits can only happen on keyframes, so clip start and end times may shift slightly.

title: Frequently Asked Questions
section: How do I fix Cannot split video due to too many scenes ?
text: On Windows, passing hundreds of scene timecodes to an external command can exceed the operating system's command-line length limit. To work around this limit, export the scene list with list-scenes and split the video in smaller batches using ffmpeg or mkvmerge directly. See Issue #164 for details.

title: Frequently Asked Questions
section: How do I fix Failed to read any frames from video file ?
text: The active video backend could not decode the file. Install PyAV ( pip install av ) and run PySceneDetect with -b pyav to test another backend. Videos with multiple audio tracks can also cause decode failures in OpenCV (see Issue #179 ). If PyAV does not help, make a copy of the video without its audio tracks. Then run detection on the copy: ffmpeg -i input.mp4 -c copy -an output.mp4 Or with mkvmerge : mkvmerge -o output.mkv --no-audio input.mp4

title: Contributing & Support
text: Report bugs and request features on the PySceneDetect issue tracker on GitHub . Before opening a new issue , search existing issues to check for known fixes or workarounds. Adding reproduction details to an existing report is also helpful.

title: Contributing & Support
text: PySceneDetect development takes place at github.com/Breakthrough/PySceneDetect . Pull requests are welcome. When possible, link each pull request to an entry on the issue tracker . Before submitting a pull request, check that your changes meet these requirements: All unit tests pass ( pytest ). Linting and formatting checks pass ( ruff check and ruff format ). New public APIs include type hints and docstrings with Arguments: / Returns: sections. When working on repository branches, use a descriptive prefix matching the change: feature/<name> , issue/<num>-<desc> , fix/<name> , docs/<name> , or

title: Contributing & Support
text: These areas are open for community contributions. Open an issue on GitHub to discuss an approach before writing a large change.

title: Contributing & Support
text: Bright flashes and fast camera movement can still trigger false cuts in some videos. Contributions that improve both accuracy and speed for these cases are welcome.

title: Contributing & Support
text: detect-content currently requires a fixed threshold. Peak-detection methods that estimate a threshold automatically (for example, --threshold=auto ) would reduce manual tuning across diverse videos.

title: Contributing & Support
text: Detection accuracy on slow dissolves varies with transition length and detector settings. Better dissolve detection with low performance overhead remains an open problem.

title: Contributing & Support
text: Research and prototypes for faster or more accurate detectors are always welcome.

title: Contributing & Support
text: A cross-platform GUI for Windows, Linux, and macOS would make PySceneDetect easier for non-technical users. No official GUI has been built yet.

title: Contributing & Support
text: PySceneDetect is currently available only in English. Contributions to support localization in the CLI, documentation, or a future GUI will help more people use PySceneDetect in their own language.

title: Contributing & Support
text: PySceneDetect is built and distributed with help from the tools, services, and contributors below. Listing these services gives credit for their support and does not imply endorsement.

title: Projects & Research
text: LTX-2 : cuts training videos into scenes with split_scenes.py . Data-Juicer : splits videos at scene changes with its video_split_by_scene_mapper operator. OneTrainer : finds cuts with AdaptiveDetector when extracting training clips. VideoX-Fun : detects cuts in its video captioning pipeline.

title: Projects & Research
text: ViMax : splits generated transition videos into shots with split_video_ffmpeg . InfiniteTalk : detects shots in input videos by combining the content, adaptive, and threshold detectors.

title: Projects & Research
text: ECC : measures the cut cadence of a reference video by sweeping ContentDetector thresholds. RAG-Anything : splits videos into scenes before indexing them. CAMEL : extracts keyframes at scene changes in VideoAnalysisToolkit . Skill Seekers : finds scene boundaries in scraped videos before extracting keyframes. OmAgent : splits videos into scenes for its video understanding agent. Pixeltable : provides scene_detect video functions with an example notebook. MassGen : extracts frames from each scene in its video extraction tool.

title: Projects & Research
text: Moondream : detects scenes before running its content moderation model. REAL Video Enhancer : includes ContentDetector to catch scene changes during rendering. movie-narrator : detects scenes as part of its movie recap pipeline.
